# Cycle 1: Parameterized Reports {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## One Report, Many Cohorts

* A health department writes the **same report** for every borough, clinic, or year.
* Copy, paste, and edit five times, and every bug needs fixing in five places.
* A **parameterized report** is written once. You choose a value (a borough, a year) and render, and every table, figure, and sentence follows.

::: {.callout-tip}
The parameter is to a report what an argument is to a function (Week 9).
:::

---

## Step 1: Declare Parameters in the YAML

```yaml
---
title: "Child Health Report"
format: html
params:
  continent: "Africa"
  year: 2015
---
```

* `params:` lists each parameter with its **default** value.
* Inside the document, R sees them as a list: `params$continent`, `params$year`.

---

## Step 2: Use `params$` Instead of Typed Values

```{r}
# Quarto creates `params` when it renders a report with a params: header.
# A slide deck has no such header, so here we create the same list by hand.
params <- list(continent = "Africa", year = 2015)

report_data <- gm |>
  filter(continent == params$continent, year == params$year,
         !is.na(life_expectancy))

nrow(report_data)
```

* Never type `"Africa"` or `2015` again below the YAML: use `params$...` everywhere.

---

## Step 3: Render Each Version from the Terminal

This command runs in RStudio's **Terminal** tab (not the R Console), so it is shown here, not run:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd -P continent:Asia -P year:2010
```

* `-P name:value` overrides one default; anything you leave out keeps its YAML value.
* Add `--output report-asia.html` to keep each version in its own file.
* Plain `quarto render report.qmd` (or the Render button) uses the defaults.

---

## The Same Idea in R: A Function

```{r}
child_health_table <- function(cont, yr) {
  stopifnot(cont %in% gm$continent)
  gm |>
    filter(continent == cont, year == yr,
           !is.na(life_expectancy), !is.na(child_mortality)) |>
    group_by(region) |>
    summarize(countries = n(),
              life_exp  = mean(life_expectancy),
              under5    = mean(child_mortality)) |>
    arrange(desc(life_exp))
}
```

* The arguments play the role of `params`: the function returns the table for **any** continent and year.
* `stopifnot()` stops early on a value that has no data, instead of returning an empty table.

---

## Calling It

```{r}
#| error: true
child_health_table("Africa", 2015)

child_health_table("Antarctica", 2015)
```

---

## Map Over Parameter Values

```{r}
conts <- c("Africa", "Americas", "Asia", "Europe", "Oceania")
tables <- map(conts, \(x) child_health_table(x, 2015))
names(tables) <- conts

map_int(tables, nrow)       # regions per continent
tables$Oceania
```

* One function, five reports' worth of tables, in three lines (`map()` from Week 9).

---

## A Plot Function, Too

```{r}
le_trend <- function(cont) {
  gm |>
    filter(continent == cont, year >= 1960, year <= 2015,
           !is.na(life_expectancy)) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarize(median_le = median(life_expectancy)) |>
    ggplot(aes(year, median_le)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = paste("Median life expectancy,", cont),
         x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)")
}
```

* The title is built from the parameter with `paste()`, so it is right for every continent.

---

## One Call, One Figure

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
le_trend("Asia")
```

---

# Cycle 2: Publication Tables with `gt` {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## A Summary Worth Publishing

NHANES adults, grouped by age:

```{r}
adults <- NHANES |>
  filter(Age >= 20) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(Age, breaks = c(20, 35, 50, 65, Inf), right = FALSE,
                         labels = c("20-34", "35-49", "50-64", "65+")))

age_summary <- adults |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
            sbp = mean(BPSysAve, na.rm = TRUE),
            diabetes = mean(Diabetes == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE))
```

* `cut()` turns a number into groups; `right = FALSE` puts age 35 in "35-49".

---

## Printed Tibbles Are for You, Not Your Reader

```{r}
age_summary
```

* Cryptic names, `<dbl>` labels, too many digits, a proportion where a reader expects a percent.
* A report needs a **table**: title, labels, units, sensible rounding, a source.

---

## `gt()`: Start a Table

```{r}
age_summary |> gt()
```

* `gt` ("grammar of tables") builds a table step by step with `|>`, like `ggplot2` builds a plot with `+`.

---

## Title and Source: `tab_header()`, `tab_source_note()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
age_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Health by age group",
    subtitle = "US adults aged 20+"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    "Source: NHANES 2009-2012 (R package NHANES)"
  )
```

---

## Format Numbers: `fmt_number()`, `fmt_integer()`, `fmt_percent()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
age_tbl <- age_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_integer(columns = n) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(bmi, sbp),
             decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = diabetes,
              decimals = 1)
age_tbl
```

* `fmt_percent()` **multiplies by 100**: give it a proportion (0.137), not a percent (13.7).
* Formatting changes the display only; the data underneath keep full precision.

---

## Readable Labels: `cols_label()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
age_tbl <- age_tbl |>
  cols_label(
    age_group = "Age group",
    n = "N",
    bmi = "BMI (kg/m²)",
    sbp = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
    diabetes = "Diabetes"
  )
age_tbl
```

* The data keep their short names; only the **displayed** labels change.

---

## Group Columns: `tab_spanner()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
age_tbl <- age_tbl |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Means",
              columns = c(bmi, sbp)) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Health by age group",
    subtitle = "US adults aged 20+"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    "Source: NHANES 2009-2012"
  )
age_tbl
```

---

## Highlight a Row: `tab_style()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
age_tbl |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#fde2e2"),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = diabetes > 0.15
    )
  )
```

* `rows =` takes a condition on the **data**, like `filter()`.
* Use emphasis sparingly: one message per table.

---

## A `gt` Recipe for Your Project

| Step | Function |
|:---|:---|
| Start from a small summary tibble | `group_by()` + `summarize()` |
| Make the table | `gt()` |
| Title, subtitle | `tab_header()` |
| Readable column names with units | `cols_label()` |
| Rounding, commas, percents | `fmt_number()`, `fmt_integer()`, `fmt_percent()` |
| Group related columns | `tab_spanner()` |
| Cite the data | `tab_source_note()` |

---

## 👥 Paired Exercise 2: Table 1 by Race/Ethnicity (10 min)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Task

1. For NHANES adults (20+), summarize by `Race1`: number of adults, mean age, mean BMI, share with diabetes, share physically active.
2. Turn it into a `gt` table with a title and subtitle.
3. Label every column, with units.
4. Format: integers for N, one decimal for means, percents for shares; a spanner over the two shares; a source note.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Checklist

* Shares stay proportions (0 to 1) until `fmt_percent()`.
* `na.rm = TRUE` inside `mean()`.
* Does any percent exceed 100%? Then something is wrong.
:::
:::


# Cycle 3: Cross-References, Inline R & `DT` {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Hand-Typed Numbers Drift

```{r}
diab_rate <- mean(adults$Diabetes == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE)
diab_rate
```

* A report says "`r round(100 * diab_rate)`% of adults have diabetes", typed by hand. Then you drop a few rows, or switch the parameter, and the sentence is **silently wrong**.
* Fix: let R write the number into the sentence. This is **inline R**.

---

## Inline R: R Writes the Numbers

What you type in the text of a `.qmd`:

```markdown
Among `r knitr::inline_expr('format(nrow(adults), big.mark = ",")')` adults, `r knitr::inline_expr('round(100 * diab_rate, 1)')`% have diabetes.
```

What the reader sees:

> Among `r format(nrow(adults), big.mark = ",")` adults, `r round(100 * diab_rate, 1)`% have diabetes.

* A backtick, the letter `r`, a space, an R expression, a closing backtick.
* Compute the number in a chunk first, and keep the inline code short.

---

## Labelling a Figure

Give the chunk a `label` that starts with `fig-` and a caption:

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-bmi-age
#| fig-cap: "BMI by age group, US adults aged 20+ (NHANES 2009-2012)."
ggplot(adults, aes(age_group, BMI)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "BMI (kg/m²)")
```

Then refer to it in the text with `@fig-bmi-age`:

```markdown
As @fig-bmi-age shows, median BMI is similar across age groups.
```

---

## The Labelled Figure

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-age
#| fig-cap: "BMI by age group, US adults aged 20+ (NHANES 2009-2012)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.7
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(adults, aes(age_group, BMI)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "BMI (kg/m²)")
```

As @fig-bmi-age shows, median BMI is similar across age groups.

---

## Why Not Just Write "the Figure Below"?

* Quarto **numbers** figures for you and turns `@fig-...` into a clickable "Figure 1".
* Add, move, or delete a figure and every number and link updates.
* The rules: the label starts with `fig-`; the chunk has a `fig-cap`; the reference is `@` plus the label, with no space.
* A typo in the reference shows up as **?@fig-...** in the rendered page: search for it before you submit.

---

## Labelling a Table

Same idea with the prefix `tbl-` and a `tbl-cap`; it works with `gt` tables:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-age
#| tbl-cap: "Diabetes by age group."
#| echo: fenced
age_summary |>
  select(age_group, n, diabetes) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = diabetes, decimals = 1)
```

---

## Referring to the Table

```markdown
@tbl-age shows that diabetes is far more common after age 50.
```

renders as:

> @tbl-age shows that diabetes is far more common after age 50.

* Put the caption in `tbl-cap` (numbered by Quarto) **or** in `tab_header()`, not both with different wording.

---

## Sections: `{#sec-...}`

```markdown
## Methods {#sec-methods}

...

The model is described in @sec-methods.
```

* Add `{#sec-name}` after a heading, then refer to it with `@sec-name`.
* Sections need numbers to be referenced: add `number-sections: true` to the YAML under `format: html:`.

| You want | Label | Caption option | Reference |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Figure | `label: fig-...` | `fig-cap:` | `@fig-...` |
| Table | `label: tbl-...` | `tbl-cap:` | `@tbl-...` |
| Section | `{#sec-...}` after heading | (the heading) | `@sec-...` |

---

## `DT`: Interactive Tables

```{r}
adults |>
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) |>        # NHANES repeats some people
  select(ID, Gender, Age, BMI, Diabetes) |>
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 5))
```

---

## `gt` or `DT`?

| | `gt` | `DT` |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Purpose | a table to **read and cite** | data to **search and sort** |
| Size | a few rows of summaries | hundreds or thousands of rows |
| Output | HTML, Word, PDF | HTML only |
| In your project | your "Table 1" and results tables | optional: let readers browse the cleaned data |

* Useful `DT` options: `pageLength =` (rows per page), `filter = "top"` (a search box per column), `rownames = FALSE`.

---

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Task

1. Compute `n_adults`, `pct_active` and `mean_sbp` in a chunk.
2. Write a sentence that reports all three with **inline R**.
3. Make a labelled figure (`fig-`) with a caption, and a labelled `gt` table (`tbl-`); refer to both in a sentence.
4. Show 100 rows of the data with `DT`, 5 rows per page, a filter box per column.

* No number in your sentences is typed by hand.
:::

# Cycle 4: Case Study + AI Corner {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## The Question

**How does diabetes prevalence among US adults rise with age and BMI, and is the pattern the same for women and men?**

A one-page, dashboard-style report with a `sex` parameter:

1. Prepare the data **once**, with a function.
2. **Key numbers** at the top, written by inline R.
3. **One figure** that answers the question, cross-referenced.
4. **One table** with the numbers behind it.
5. Render for each sex: `-P sex:female`, `-P sex:male`.

---

## Step 1: Prepare the Data with a Function

```{r}
prep_adults <- function(data, sex) {
  stopifnot(sex %in% c("female", "male"))
  data |>
    filter(Age >= 20, Gender == sex, !is.na(Diabetes), !is.na(BMI)) |>
    mutate(age_group = cut(Age, breaks = c(20, 35, 50, 65, Inf), right = FALSE,
                           labels = c("20-34", "35-49", "50-64", "65+")),
           obese = BMI >= 30)
}

params <- list(sex = "female")     # in the report, from the YAML
cohort <- prep_adults(NHANES, params$sex)
nrow(cohort)
```

---

## Step 2: Key Numbers, Written by R

```{r}
key <- cohort |>
  summarize(n = n(), diabetes = mean(Diabetes == "Yes"), obese = mean(obese))
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Adults in the cohort**

[`r format(key$n, big.mark = ",")`]{style="font-size: 1.8em"}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**With diabetes**

[`r round(100 * key$diabetes, 1)`%]{style="font-size: 1.8em"}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**With obesity (BMI 30+)**

[`r round(100 * key$obese, 1)`%]{style="font-size: 1.8em"}
:::
:::
:::

* Each big number is inline R, so it changes when `sex` changes.

---

## Step 3: The Figure

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
cohort |>
  group_by(age_group, obese) |>
  summarize(diabetes = mean(Diabetes == "Yes"), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(bmi_group = if_else(obese, "BMI 30+", "BMI under 30")) |>
  ggplot(aes(age_group, diabetes, fill = bmi_group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "With diabetes", fill = NULL,
       title = paste("Diabetes by age and BMI,", params$sex, "adults"))
```

---

## Step 4: The Table Behind It

```{r}
#| output-location: column
cohort |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    obese = mean(obese),
    diab = mean(Diabetes == "Yes")
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(age_group = "Age group",
             n = "N",
             obese = "BMI 30+",
             diab = "Diabetes") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(obese, diab),
              decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(paste("Adults:",
                   params$sex))
```

---

## Step 5: Every Value of the Parameter

```{r}
key_numbers <- function(sex) {
  prep_adults(NHANES, sex) |>
    summarize(sex = sex, n = n(),
              diabetes = mean(Diabetes == "Yes"), obese = mean(obese))
}

map(c("female", "male"), key_numbers) |>
  bind_rows()
```

* In the report, `quarto render report.qmd -P sex:male` gives the whole page for men.
* NHANES in R is resampled for teaching: describe patterns in this sample, not official US rates.

---

## Quarto Dashboards (Optional)

Quarto can also lay a report out as a dashboard. Shown here, not run:

```yaml
---
title: "Diabetes Dashboard"
format: dashboard
params:
  sex: "female"
---
```

* Each `##` heading becomes a **row** of cards; each chunk's output becomes a card.
* Your final project is an ordinary `format: html` report; everything today (params, `gt`, cross-references, inline R) works there.

---

## Checklist for Your Project Report

* **Tables:** at least one `gt` table, labelled `tbl-` and referenced in the text.
* **Figures:** each labelled `fig-` with a `fig-cap`, each referenced with `@fig-...`.
* **Numbers in sentences:** inline R, never typed by hand (this is in the rubric).
* **Repeated work:** a function, used more than once, and `map()` over groups.
* **Render** from top to bottom, then search the page for `?@` and for `NA`.


## AI Corner: The Table That Is Off by 100x {background-color="#8e44ad"}

Asked to "make a publication-ready table of diabetes prevalence by age group," an AI wrote:

```{r}
ai_summary <- adults |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            pct_diabetes = 100 * mean(Diabetes == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE))

ai_tbl <- ai_summary |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(age_group = "Age group", n = "N",
             pct_diabetes = "Diabetes prevalence") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = pct_diabetes, decimals = 1)
```

Clean code, nice labels, `fmt_percent()` as taught. Ship it?

## AI Corner: Look at the Output {background-color="#8e44ad"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ai_tbl
```

## AI Corner: Auditing the Table {background-color="#8e44ad"}

**Audit findings:**

```{r}
range(ai_summary$pct_diabetes)
```

1. The AI already multiplied by 100, then `fmt_percent()` multiplied by 100 **again**.
2. Every prevalence is 100 times too large: the oldest group shows `r format(round(100 * max(ai_summary$pct_diabetes), 1), big.mark = ",")`%, which is impossible.
3. A reader skimming the table, or an AI summarizing it, could repeat that number without noticing.

## AI Corner: The Audited Version {background-color="#8e44ad"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
adults |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            diabetes = mean(Diabetes == "Yes",
                            na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(age_group = "Age group",
             n = "N",
             diabetes = "Diabetes prevalence") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = diabetes,
              decimals = 1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
* Keep proportions (0 to 1) in the data; let `fmt_percent()` do the 100x **once**.
* Check: is every percent between 0% and 100%? Does one cell match a number you computed yourself?

::: {.callout-important}
*Read the rendered table, not just the code.*
:::
:::
:::

---
